desc:
There are n cities labelled 1 to n. Each entry roads[i] = [a, b, w] is a two-way road between cities a and b with quality w (larger means better).

A route from city 1 to city n is any walk along roads; it may pass through the same city or road more than once. The weakness of a route is the smallest quality of any road on it.

Return the smallest weakness that any route from city 1 to city n can have (the worst route you could be made to take). If no route exists, return -1.

n = 4, roads = [[1,2,9],[2,3,6],[2,4,5],[1,4,7]]

result = 5     (route 1-2-4 uses the quality-5 road; no route can be weaker)
constraints: 1 ≤ a, b ≤ n and a ≠ b
No pair of cities appears twice
hints: Because a route may wander and reuse roads, a route can detour through any road that is connected to the path.
So which roads can appear on some route from 1 to n? Exactly the roads in the connected component that contains both city 1 and city n.
Union the endpoints of all roads. If cities 1 and n have different roots, answer -1. Otherwise the answer is the minimum w over all roads whose endpoint has the same root as city 1.
editorial: Since walks may revisit cities, any road in the same connected component as city 1 can be included in a route from 1 to n (walk to it, cross it, come back, continue to n) as long as n is also in that component. Hence the answer is simply the smallest road weight inside that component.

Union all roads. If find(1) != find(n), return -1. Otherwise scan the roads once more and take the minimum weight among those with find(a) == find(1). Time O((n + m) · α(n)). A BFS from city 1 works equally well; the point is to recognise that the question is about connectivity, not about shortest paths.
